In a detailed report,Next also warned of the challenges to the wider UK economy,cautioning that growth was likely to slow as "employer tax increases, and their potential impact on prices and 
employment, begin to filter through into the company".
Next said the rise in national insurance for employers "creates a disproportionate increase in the cost of part-time work in stores", which makes up a significant proportion of employment across the

industry. To highlight the point, Next included a table in its trading update which showed the national insurance changes on three levels of salaries.The graph showed that a £9,520 part-time national living wage salary will increase by 6.5 per cent, while a full-time wage of £22.310 would increase by 3.5 per cent and a £60,000 salary by 2 per cent.
Higher costs of employing low-paid,part-time workers could deter retailers from hiring, reducing opportunities for those
seeking flexible roles to re-enter the workforce. This risks undermining social mobility and getting more people back into the workplace.

The high street leader has added to a growing number of retail businesses,including AO and Currys, warning over price rises to combat cost increases. The British Chambers of Commerce said earlier this week that more than half of companies were planning to lift prices over the next three months due to cost pressures.
Asda trails  the pack for  festive sales
Emma Taggart
Debt-laden Asda was the worst-performing supermarket chain over the Christmas period.

The private equity-controlled group suffered a 5.8 per cent fall in sales in the 12 weeks to December 29, driving its market share down from 13.5 per cent to 12.5 per cent, data from the market research group Kantar showed.
Asda said it had seen improvements to its sales and market share in the four weeks to December 29 compared with the same period in 2023.

The Leeds-based grocer has struggled with slowing sales since it was bought by the private equity firm TDR and the billionaire Issa brothers in 2021in a highly leveraged £6.8 billion takeover deal. Asda's large debt pile has also prevented it from keeping up with lower-priced competitors such as the German discounters Aldi and Lidl.

In November Lord Rose of Monewden, then chairman of Asda, admitted that the group had "not been as sharp on our trading stance as we should have been … we have lost a bit of market share and a bit of momentum".

The fall in Asda's market share comes as inflation across supermarkets climbed to its highest level since March last year. Grocery price inflation rose to 3.7 per cent last month, up from 2.6 per cent in November, according to Kantar.
Overall grocery sales climbed 2.l per cent in the four weeks to December 29.as households spent an average of £460on groceries during the period.

Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at Kantar, said:"It was a solid Christmas at the supermarkets with sales surpassing £l3 billion during the four weeks of December for the first time ever."

Tesco continued to solidify its position as Britain's biggest supermarket chain as it grew its market share by 0.8 percentage points to 28.5 per cent in 12 weeks to December 29. Sales rose 5 per cent in the festive period.

Sainsbury's reported its largest market share since December 20l9 at 16 per cent. Sales at Britain's second biggest supermarket group outpaced the wider market to rise 3.5 per cent in the 12 weeks to December 29.
The German discount chains Aldi and Lidl both recorded their highest market share for the festive quarter, at 10 per cent and 7.3 per cent respectively.
Telegraph  boss thought  sale would  gq quicker
James Hurley
The chief executive of Telegraph Media Group has sought to reassure staff after the newspaper's editor warned of an "inevitable sense of drift"  over the protracted auction of the business.
Anna Jones, who took over last year amid a potential sale of The Telegraph,admitted that the group's executives thought that an acquisition of the newspaper would have been "done and dusted" by now.
She said that there was "lots of pressure" on the business as a result of a sale
process, which was called "the newspaper auction from hell"  by the Columbia Journalism Review, but said staff were able to "shut out the noise".

Jones's intervention followed a new year message to staff from Chris Evans,The Telegraph's editor-in-chief, in which he described the situation as unsatisfactory. "Last year was supposed to be the year when The Telegraph was sold. We were told we would be sold by the summer, then by autumn and, at the latest, by Christmas," he wrote. "But …we don't know when it might be sold."
He added: "There's obviously a limit to what we can do in these circumstances but we're going to try to do everything we can to recover momentum and to defeat the inevitable sense of drift."

RedBird IMI, a venture part-funded by an Emirati royal, has been in control of The Telegraph's future for nearly eight months but is struggling to find a buyer. The fund is seeking full repayment of the money it initially invested in the debt secured against The Telegraph and The Spectator, its sister publication, which was part of a plan for a full takeover of the titles.

Ministers blocked its attempts to convert its debt into equity ownership amid concerns about foreign powers buying UK media assets. RedBird IMI sold The Spectator to Paul Marshall, the GB News owner, for f£lo0 million but is seeking to recoup a total of £600 million.Lord Saatchi said RedBird had "overpaid" when his £350 million offer for The Telegraph was rejected in August.
The Telegraph has reported calls from senior politicians for Lisa Nandy,the culture secretary, to intervene.

Yesterday Jones wrote on LinkedIn:"The Telegraph Media Group has been for sale for 18 months now and I've been CEO for almost a year. To be candid, we thought it would be done and dusted within six months."

Jones, a former chief executive of Hearst Magazines, added: "As someone who's been through these processes before and understands how challenging it can be … I remind everyone that yes there's lots of pressure but not all of it is real …. Listening to too many outside voices can become exhausting so we've been mindful to shut out the noise and focus on creating our own destiny."
